comparison: Both strongly support the screening methodology and findings (C22-C29). OpenEval emphasizes technical aspects like controls and statistical analysis, while peer reviewers praise the normality score as 'robust' and note the data will be 'helpful to the wider community.' Complete agreement on screening validity.

Both support the FRAP analysis and biophysical characterization (C62-C68, C123-C127). OpenEval provides detailed technical validation of the FRAP methodology and interpretations about LLPS complexity. Peer reviewers commend 'high quality imaging and quantitative data' without raising concerns. Full agreement on biophysical findings.

Significant disagreement on mechanistic conclusions (C7, C76, C80-C82, C100-C101, C117). OpenEval finds the CDK9-Treacle-POLR1A mechanism well-supported with strong evidence. Peer reviewers rate as UNCERTAIN, stating 'mechanistic exploration of CDK9i is not sufficiently developed' and requesting additional ChIP experiments and Treacle mutant validation.

Both support the translational implications and broader significance (C85-C87, C133, C142). OpenEval emphasizes the justification for considering nucleolar stress in drug development. Peer reviewers affirm findings are 'of broad interest' and 'valuable to the broader scientific community.' Agreement on clinical and translational relevance.

Both support the live-cell imaging validation of the normality score (C16-C20). OpenEval emphasizes how differential responses of nucleolin and UBF validate the metric. Peer reviewers praise 'high quality imaging and quantitative data' without concerns. Also partial overlap on C3 with peer R1. Agreement on imaging quality and validation.

Both support the CDK inhibitor specificity data and α-amanitin controls (C48-C53). OpenEval emphasizes how α-amanitin controls rule out indirect RNA Pol II effects. Peer reviewers acknowledge these as 'solid' observational findings, though they request additional ChIP experiments for deeper mechanistic validation. Agreement on experimental observations.

Both support the interpretive framework about nucleolar organization complexity (C69-C71, C128). OpenEval finds the LLPS interpretations appropriately cautious and well-supported. Peer reviewers implicitly accept these biophysical interpretations through praise of the data quality. Agreement on organizational complexity beyond simple LLPS.

Both support the classification of distinct stress states (C72-C75, C129). OpenEval finds the four-state classification well-supported by morphological, molecular, and biophysical data. Peer reviewers explicitly affirm the 'novel finding that different chemotherapeutic agents can induce nucleolar stress' with varying characteristics. Strong agreement on stress state classification.

Disagreement on mechanistic evidence sufficiency (C54-C55, C58, C112-C113). OpenEval finds the phosphoproteomics, kinase assays, and Treacle identification strongly supported. Peer reviewers rate as UNCERTAIN, stating mechanistic exploration 'not sufficiently developed' and requesting PolI ChIP and Treacle mutant experiments to strengthen claims.

Both support the characterization of distinct stress states using multiple approaches (C33, C35, C37, C40). OpenEval emphasizes comprehensive multi-method validation. Peer reviewers affirm these characterization findings as 'solid and valuable.' Agreement on experimental characterization quality.

Both support the reversibility and dynamic imaging data (C41-C43). OpenEval notes reversibility of CDK inhibitor effects strengthens mechanistic interpretations. Peer reviewers praise 'high quality imaging and quantitative data' without concerns. Agreement on dynamic characterization.

Disagreement on interaction data sufficiency (C61, C116). OpenEval finds the loss of Treacle-POLR1A interaction strongly supports phosphorylation-dependent mechanism. Peer reviewers question sufficiency, requesting PolI ChIP on rDNA and Treacle mutant experiments to adequately establish mechanistic relevance.

Minimal overlap on C3 (nucleolar normality score). OpenEval groups C3 with extensive validation claims (C16-C21). Peer R1 groups C3 with screening claims (C22-C29). Both support the normality score but in different contexts - OpenEval focuses on validation, peer reviewers on screening application.

Both support the contradiction of prior work (C79) and α-amanitin control data. OpenEval emphasizes how controls directly contradict Abraham et al. 2020. Peer reviewers accept these observational findings as part of solid conclusions, though request additional mechanistic validation.

OpenEval supports the contextualization and limitation acknowledgments (C134-C141) including CDK specificity challenges and potential redundancy. No corresponding peer review evaluation found for these specific discussion/limitation claims.

OpenEval supports the background and established knowledge claims (C1-C2, C8-C15, C46-C47, C88-C97) as appropriately cited. No corresponding peer review evaluation found specifically addressing these background/literature claims.
